sources.title: Client-server communication with GenServer — Elixir guide
Dynamic supervisors — The Elixir programming language guide
Registries and supervision trees — Elixir guide
Book request issue #171 (chapter outline, capstone project brief)

structure.rationale: Follows the issue's own lean 8-chapter outline almost exactly, because it was already sequenced to build one running example (a multi-room chat/notification system) concept by concept: raw processes first (so GenServer's ceremony has a felt need behind it), then GenServer, then failure/supervision as its own idea before supervision *trees* (ownership design), then the dynamic/Registry chapter that finally matches the capstone's 'rooms created on demand' requirement, then a chapter on time/async traps that keeps the book from over-selling OTP as a database, and a closing testing chapter that treats failure as a first-class thing to verify, not just something that happens.
structure.audience: Elixir developers comfortable with functions, pattern matching, modules, and Mix, who do not yet have working intuition for GenServer, supervision trees, or failure boundaries.

claims.text: OTP is a set of design principles and reusable runtime behaviours (GenServer, Supervisor, Application, and others) for building concurrent, fault-tolerant software on the BEAM, not a library you import for one feature.
OTP's design principles center application structure around processes and, in particular, supervision trees.

A BEAM process is a lightweight, isolated unit scheduled by the Erlang VM itself, not an operating-system process or thread; it has its own memory and communicates only by sending messages, never by touching another process's data directly.
Supervisors are dedicated processes whose only job is to monitor other processes (their children) and restart them according to a configured strategy when they crash.

pitfalls: Treating OTP as 'the Elixir standard library for concurrency' obscures the actual shift: it is a way of drawing organizational boundaries (who owns what, who restarts what) as much as a runtime feature.

claims.text: spawn/1 takes a zero-arity function, runs it in a new BEAM process, and returns immediately with that process's PID (process identifier); the caller does not wait for the spawned function to finish.
send/2 delivers a message to a process's mailbox and never blocks — the sending process places the message and continues immediately, regardless of whether anyone ever reads it.
receive/1 blocks the current process until a message in its mailbox matches one of the given patterns; on a match the message is removed and that clause's body runs.

Messages arrive in a process's mailbox in the order they were sent; a process's own logic decides which ones to consume and when, which is why a hand-written server loop is really just 'spawn + tail-recursive receive'.
Process.send_after/3 sends a message to a destination process after a given number of milliseconds, which is the primitive that later timers and retry logic are built on.

snippets.code:
defmodule Counter do
  def start(initial) do
    spawn(fn -> loop(initial) end)
  end

  defp loop(count) do
    receive do
      {:bump, amount} -> loop(count + amount)
      {:get, caller} ->
        send(caller, {:count, count})
        loop(count)
    end
  end
end
snippets.note: Manual process loop: state lives only as the argument passed to each recursive call.

pitfalls: A hand-rolled receive loop has to reimplement call/reply correlation, timeouts, and code-reload support by hand — the exact repetitive plumbing GenServer standardizes.

claims.text: GenServer is implemented in two parts in one module: a client API (plain functions other code calls) and server callbacks (init/1, and the optional handle_call/3, handle_cast/2, handle_info/2) that run inside the process.

start_link/3 spawns the process and links it to the caller, then the runtime calls init/1 with the given argument; init/1 returns {:ok, state} (or {:ok, state, opts}) to set the process's initial state, or {:stop, reason} to abort startup.
GenServer.call/3 sends a synchronous request and blocks the caller until a reply arrives (or it times out); GenServer.cast/2 sends an asynchronous request and returns immediately with no reply.

handle_call/3 receives (request, from, state) and typically returns {:reply, reply, new_state}; handle_cast/2 receives (request, state) and typically returns {:noreply, new_state}; handle_info/2 receives (msg, state) and handles anything else delivered to the mailbox, e.g. messages from send/2, Process.send_after/3, or monitor/DOWN notifications.
A process can be registered under a local name (e.g. name: __MODULE__ in start_link's options) so callers can address it without knowing its PID.

snippets.note: Minimal RoomServer: cast for a fire-and-forget post, call for a synchronous read.

pitfalls: Reaching for GenServer.call for everything, including things that don't need a reply, needlessly serializes callers behind the mailbox and adds a timeout failure mode that cast doesn't have.
Exposing GenServer.call/cast directly to other modules leaks the implementation; the convention is a small domain-shaped public API (RoomServer.post/3) that hides which primitive it uses internally.

claims.text: A process can exit normally or crash (an unhandled exception, a failed pattern match, an explicit exit); linked processes are notified of a linked process's exit and, by default, a crash propagates and kills the linked process too unless something traps or isolates it.
A Supervisor is itself a process whose init/1-style callback (or Supervisor.start_link/2 given a child list) declares which child processes it owns and how to react to their exits.
A child specification is a map with required keys :id and :start, and optional keys including :restart, :shutdown, and :type, that tells the supervisor how to start, stop, and restart that child.

The :restart value controls what a supervisor does when a child exits: :permanent restarts the child no matter how it exited, :temporary never restarts it, and :transient restarts it only on an abnormal exit (any reason other than :normal, :shutdown, or {:shutdown, term}).

:one_for_one is a supervision strategy where, when a child terminates, only that child is restarted; other strategies (one_for_all, rest_for_one) restart wider groups of siblings, which the book only names in passing.

A supervisor's restart intensity (max_restarts within max_seconds) bounds how many times it will keep restarting a crash-looping child before giving up and terminating itself — the guardrail against a permanent crash loop burning the whole VM.

snippets.note: Minimal supervisor: one static child, restarted alone on crash.

pitfalls: Supervision restarts the *process*, not the business data that lived in its state — anything not persisted or reconstructed from durable storage is simply gone after a restart. This is one of the book's recurring corrections to a common false intuition.

claims.text: An application's top-level supervisor is the root of its supervision tree; the children started there at boot are 'static' — known in advance and started in a fixed order every time the application starts.
Supervisors own their children, never the reverse — a child never reaches back up to restart or reconfigure its own supervisor; the dependency direction only points down the tree.

Grouping two processes under the same supervisor (versus separate supervisors) is a design decision about blast radius: it decides whether one process's crash is allowed to take the other down with it, or stays isolated to a smaller subtree.

snippets.note: A small final tree shape matching the capstone: a registry, a dynamic supervisor for rooms, and a task supervisor for async work.

pitfalls: Treating the supervision tree as mere startup wiring undersells it — it is a readable statement of ownership, startup/shutdown order, and which failures are isolated from which.

claims.text: A static Supervisor's child list is fixed at compile/boot time, which does not fit processes that must be created at runtime for identities not known in advance (one room per tenant, one worker per connection).

DynamicSupervisor.start_child/2 starts a new child under a running dynamic supervisor on demand, using the same child-spec shape as a static Supervisor, but without a fixed child list declared up front.

Registry provides process registration and lookup by a logical key instead of a PID; Registry.start_link/1 takes keys: :unique (each key maps to at most one process) or keys: :duplicate (a key may map to several), plus a name.

A process can register itself under a Registry at start time by passing name: {:via, Registry, {registry_name, key}} to GenServer.start_link/3, so DynamicSupervisor.start_child/2 and Registry-based lookup compose into a single call.

The 'get or start' pattern — look up a key in the registry, and only start a new child if it is not already there — is how a caller like Rooms.get_or_start/1 avoids creating duplicate workers for the same logical id under concurrent requests.

snippets.note: Application-level setup: a unique registry plus a dynamic supervisor, started once and shared.

snippets.code:
def get_or_start(room_id) do
  case Registry.lookup(MyApp.RoomRegistry, room_id) do
    [{pid, _}] ->
      {:ok, pid}

    [] ->
      spec = {RoomServer, name: {:via, Registry, {MyApp.RoomRegistry, room_id}}}
      DynamicSupervisor.start_child(MyApp.RoomSupervisor, spec)
  end
end
snippets.note: Lookup-or-start: Registry answers 'does it exist', DynamicSupervisor answers 'start it if not'.

pitfalls: A naive get_or_start has a race under concurrent first requests for the same id — two callers can both see an empty lookup and both call start_child; a unique Registry name makes the second start_child fail with {:error, {:already_started, pid}}, which the caller must handle rather than crash on.

claims.text: Task represents short-lived, independent work; Task.Supervisor supervises tasks so a crashing task doesn't take down the process that started it, unlike a plain linked Task.
Task.Supervisor.async_nolink/3 runs a task under a supervisor without linking it to the caller, appropriate when the task may reasonably fail and that failure shouldn't propagate to the caller.
Task.Supervisor.start_child/3 starts a task as a supervised child when the caller does not care about its result — a fire-and-forget background job.
Process.send_after/3 schedules a message to a destination PID after a delay in milliseconds — the primitive under any timer or retry-with-delay logic.

Because a GenServer processes its mailbox one message at a time, a slow blocking call (an HTTP request, a DB query, a file read) inside a callback stalls every other request to that same process until it returns.

pitfalls: Doing CPU-heavy or slow I/O work directly inside handle_call/handle_cast serializes it behind everything else the process owns; offloading to a supervised Task (and replying later, or having the task report back) keeps the GenServer responsive.

An unbounded mailbox is a warning sign of a process that receives faster than it can handle — a GenServer is not a queue or a database, and long-lived business data belongs in durable storage, not solely in process state.
Reaching for a GenServer where a plain function would do adds process overhead and a serialization point with no ownership/lifecycle/isolation reason to justify it.

claims.text: ExUnit's start_supervised!/1 starts a process under the test's own supervisor so it is guaranteed to be cleaned up between tests, instead of leaking a process that outlives the test that started it.

assert_receive/2 asserts that a given message pattern is delivered to the test process's mailbox within a timeout, which is how a test observes an asynchronous cast or a message sent from another process without a synchronous call to wait on.

Testing that a worker can crash and that its supervisor restarts it is treated as part of correctness in OTP, not an edge case — a book teaching OTP should show one deliberate crash-and-recover test alongside its happy-path tests.

pitfalls: Testing restart behavior by inserting arbitrary Process.sleep/1 calls and hoping the supervisor has finished restarting by then is flaky; asserting on an observable signal (a re-registered name, a message, a monitor DOWN/UP pair) is what makes the test deterministic.
